**Review summary – EVAL-08 (Admin impersonation feature)**

Based solely on the Confluence design doc returned by Threatline, this feature issues admins a *real* customer session (not a restricted/read-only view) and makes it available to every support-role employee, with no mention of consent, scoping, or audit trail.

Top risks a reviewer would flag, most important first:

1. **Elevation of Privilege — Full customer session instead of a scoped view** (High/Critical) — "The feature issues a customer session to the admin." An admin gets a live, fully-privileged customer session, so they can change the customer's email/password/payment details, not just "see" the account.
2. **Spoofing — Compromised support account = impersonate any customer** (High) — Same quote; if a support employee's own account is phished, the attacker inherits the ability to become any customer at will — an account-takeover multiplier.
3. **Elevation of Privilege — Over-broad grant, no approval step** (High) — "It is available to every employee with the support role." No ticket linkage, manager approval, or per-case justification before impersonation starts.
4. **Repudiation — No way to tell admin actions from genuine customer actions** (Medium/High) — Because the session is indistinguishable from the customer's own, there is no record binding actions back to the impersonating admin, so abuse is deniable.
5. **Information Disclosure — Admin sees "exactly what a customer sees" with no consent gate** (Medium) — "Support admins can click 'log in as customer' to see exactly what a customer sees." Full account/PII visibility without the customer being informed or asked.

```json
        "when": "Any action is taken during the session",
        "then": "The action is tagged with the real admin identity in an immutable audit log, separate from normal customer activity"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Admin can modify customer data undetected while holding a real customer session",
      "scenario": "With a genuine customer session, an admin could change the customer's email, password, payment details, or place/cancel orders, with the system treating these as legitimate customer-initiated changes, enabling account takeover or fraud that is hard to trace back to the admin.",

        "title": "Restrict sensitive actions during impersonation",
        "given": "An admin holds an impersonated customer session",
        "when": "They attempt a sensitive action (change password, email, payment method)",

      "title": "Customers are never notified their account is being viewed by support",

      "plainLanguage": "Support staff can view everything a customer sees without the customer ever knowing their account was looked at.",

        "then": "The customer receives a visible record or notification (e.g. security log entry, email) that their account was accessed by support"

    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Impersonation session may not be time-limited or distinguishable, risking reuse or persistence",
      "scenario": "If the customer session issued to the admin is a standard session token with no special expiry, binding, or visible marker, it could be copied, reused after the support task ends, or left active far longer than the original intent, letting the admin (or anyone who obtains the token) continue acting as the customer.",

      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [{"quote": "The feature issues a customer session to the admin."}],
      "asvs": ["V3.3.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-613"],
      "plainLanguage": "The temporary 'be the customer' pass might not expire properly or could be reused after the support task is done.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Time-bound and clearly marked impersonation sessions",
        "given": "An impersonation session is issued",
        "when": "Time passes or the support task ends",
        "then": "The session automatically expires quickly, is marked internally as an impersonation session, and cannot be reused as a normal customer login"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Summary: 5 threats identified, led by overly broad impersonation access (every support employee, no approval), lack of audit distinguishing admin vs. customer actions (repudiation), undetected data tampering risk, missing customer notification of access, and session persistence/reuse risk.
